bonds.title: The cook in the smoke
bonds.where: Omoide Yokocho, by the west exit
bonds.busy: Charcoal's not lit. Come back in the evening, or late: we grill till the last train.

ranks.title: Salt or sauce
ranks.invite: You stood in the smoke and didn't cough. Got a bit of the {slot}? Sit. I'll tell you why we grill what we grill.
talk: After the war flour and rice were rationed, and offal wasn't. So the stalls here grilled offal on sticks. That's how this lane started, in 1946.
Chicken came later. We call all of it yakitori anyway. Order pork here and that's what the menu will call it.
ranks.fact: Omoide Yokocho began about 1946 as a black market by Shinjuku Station's west exit, whose stalls grilled offal because it was not a rationed food.

options.reply: Ha. Right answer: ask the cook. Salt for the first one, so you taste the bird. Sauce after.
It's your skewer. Try the first with salt, though: you'll taste the bird.

request.ask: Eaten yet? Not from a convenience store. Sit at a counter somewhere, then come and tell me.

ranks.title: A run to Golden Gai
talk: Good. You eat like you mean it.
Eighty-odd shops in this lane, and most seat eight. Fumi's bar over in Golden Gai seats six, and she feeds them my skewers.
I need legs. A box for her counter, while they're hot. It pays, and she'll tell me if you dawdled.
ranks.fact: Omoide Yokocho, Memory Lane, packs about eighty small shops, most of them grills and counters, into the lanes beside the tracks at Shinjuku's west exit.

gives.name: Kenta's runner
gives.text: A paid delivery from the grill, in your diary under Work

request.text: Run the skewers to Fumi's bar in Golden Gai
request.ask: The box is packed and getting cold. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The busiest station
talk: Fumi says they arrived hot. From her that's a speech.
About three and a half million people a day go through the station behind that wall. More than any other station on earth: it's in the record books.
Over two hundred exits. Eleven years I've worked here, and I still come up out of the wrong one.
ranks.fact: Shinjuku Station handles about 3.5 million passengers a day, the most of any station in the world by Guinness World Records, and has more than 200 exits.

ask.q: Which exit did you come out of, your first time?

options.text: No idea. I followed the crowd
options.reply: Honest. That's how everyone does it. Next time, follow the smoke.
Nobody does, the first time. Next time, follow the smoke.

request.text: Guess a tower's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: The towers past the tracks: how tall, d'you reckon? Pick one, press G, and tell me how close you were.

ranks.title: 243 metres
talk: Not bad. The twin-topped one is the city government's: 243 metres, opened in 1991, and it's free to go up.
Everything out west is that size. In here it's the other way: my counter seats eight, and in places you can touch both walls of the lane.
ranks.fact: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building in Nishi-Shinjuku, by Tange Kenzo, opened in 1991 and stands 243 m tall, with free observation rooms 202 m up.

gives.name: A cook's tongue
gives.text: Taste: you know a good counter when you smell one

request.ask: Try a few more counters. The department store's basement, a coffee shop's morning set. Then come back.

ranks.title: The smoke stays
talk: They keep drawing new towers round us. The big one across the road is due in the spring of 2030: 258 metres of it.
The lane's still here. Come when it rains: the smoke hangs under the roofs and the whole place smells of charcoal and soy.
Your seat's the one by the grill. Hottest in the house. It's an honour, I promise.
ranks.fact: A 48-storey, 258 m tower is going up over Shinjuku Station's west exit, where the Odakyu department store stood until 2022, for completion by March 2030.

gives.name: The seat by the grill
gives.text: 15% more for every job in Shinjuku

bonds.title: Six seats in Golden Gai
bonds.where: Golden Gai, where the lanes meet the promenade
bonds.busy: The bar's shut till dark. Come at night: these lanes don't wake before seven.

ranks.title: Six seats
ranks.invite: You read the door before you came in. Good. Have you the {slot}? Take the end stool; the middle ones are spoken for.
talk: Golden Gai was moved here, you know. The stalls stood by the station until the black markets were ordered cleared in 1949. They carried the whole trade up the road.
Two storeys of wood and a stair like a ladder. I've kept six seats here for forty years.
ranks.fact: Golden Gai's bars descend from a black market near Shinjuku Station that was ordered cleared in 1949 and moved to this block beside Hanazono Shrine.

ask.q: Why are the bars so small, do you think?

options.text: Each one was a market stall's plot
options.reply: Just so. One stall, one patch of ground, a dozen square metres or so. Nobody ever joined two together.
Rent's the least of it. Each bar is one market stall's patch of ground, and nobody ever joined two together.

request.text: Pay your respects at Hanazono Shrine after dark
request.ask: Have you been up to Hanazono yet? Go at night, when the lanterns are lit. It's behind us.

ranks.title: The red tent
talk: You went. Then you stood where the red tent stood.
In 1967 a playwright called Kara Juro pitched a red tent in the shrine's yard and staged what no theatre would have. Half his audience drank here afterwards.
The cab drivers drink here too, when they come off at four. I've told them about you.
ranks.fact: In 1967 the playwright Kara Juro's Situation Theatre first pitched its red tent in the grounds of Hanazono Shrine, a landmark of Japan's underground theatre.

gives.name: Fumi's word with the night drivers
gives.text: 25% off every taxi and ride in Shinjuku

request.text: Take a taxi (a hand up at the kerb, Y)
request.ask: Have you tried a cab yet? A hand up at the kerb. Tell me whether he was civil.

ranks.title: The men with money
talk: Civil? Good. I told them you tip in conversation.
In the eighties men came down these lanes with cash to buy us out, and some tried worse than cash. We took turns walking the lanes at night.
So we're still two storeys of wood. Everything round us went up thirty floors.
ranks.fact: In the land boom of the 1980s developers tried to buy out Golden Gai; its owners organised to resist, and the low wooden lanes survived.

options.text: Not while the regulars had nowhere else
options.reply: That's what I told the man with the briefcase. Almost word for word.
Honest of you. A few did. I decided the stools were worth more with people on them.

request.text: Photograph the lanes of Golden Gai (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Take me a picture of the lanes. Photo mode, from the promenade end. I've never once seen them from outside.

ranks.title: Who sat there
talk: Let me see. Yes. That's how it looks at one in the morning.
Writers, directors, a prize-winner or two before they had the prize. This is where film people argued until the first train.
Your stool had a novelist on it most Thursdays for nine years. I won't say which.
ranks.fact: Golden Gai holds more than 200 tiny bars in six narrow lanes, and has long been a haunt of writers, film-makers and actors.

gives.name: The lanes by heart
gives.text: Bearings: you know the back ways

ranks.title: Last orders
talk: I'm seventy-one. One day this counter will want someone who knows where the good ice is kept, and when to say nothing.
Not you. You talk too much. But you'd do for a Tuesday.
Whatever you become: learn people's drinks and never their business. That's the whole trade.
ranks.fact: Hanazono Shrine, beside Golden Gai, has been Shinjuku's guardian shrine since the Edo period, when the district was the post town of Naito-Shinjuku.

gives.name: Fumi's introduction
gives.text: 20% more for every job in Shinjuku

bonds.title: The volunteer in the rain
bonds.where: Shinjuku Gyoen, the shelter by the pond

places.where: By the Taiwan Pavilion, when it's dry

bonds.busy: Not today, dear. I sit in the shelter when it rains, mornings and middays. Never a Monday: the garden's shut.

ranks.title: Rain on the pond
ranks.invite: You came out in the rain on purpose. So do I. Have you the {slot}? This end of the bench is dry.
talk: Listen. On the pond it's one sound, on the maples another, on this roof a third. I've had twelve years to tell them apart.
This was a lord's estate: the Naito family's, from 1591. The post town that opened by their wall was called Naito-Shinjuku, and the name outlived them.
ranks.fact: Shinjuku Gyoen stands on the Edo estate of the Naito lords; the post town opened beside it in 1698 was Naito-Shinjuku, which gave Shinjuku its name.

options.reply: Just so: shin, new; juku, a post town and its inns. The new stop on the road west to Kofu.
A nice thought, with all these trees. But juku is a post town and its inns: the new stop on the road west.

request.text: Photograph the Kyu-Goryotei across the pond (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Would you take a picture of the pavilion across the water for me? My hands shake now. Photo mode, from this bank.

ranks.title: Three gardens
talk: Oh, that's lovely. You caught it in the water too.
It's three gardens, really: this Japanese one, an English lawn, and a French one with rows of plane trees. It was finished in 1906, for the imperial family.
It opened to everyone in 1949. My mother brought me the year after. I remember the lawn and nothing else.
ranks.fact: Shinjuku Gyoen was completed in 1906 as an imperial garden and opened to the public in 1949; its 58 hectares hold Japanese, English landscape and French formal gardens.

request.text: Sit in the shelter in the morning, before the garden fills
request.ask: Come and sit in the shelter early one morning, wet or dry. You'll hear what I mean.

ranks.title: No sake under the blossom
talk: Early, isn't it? Crows, the Chuo Line, and nothing else.
In spring there are about a thousand cherry trees here, of some sixty-five kinds, so something is in flower from February to late April.
And no drink. They look in your bag at the gate. It's the one quiet hanami in Tokyo.
ranks.fact: Shinjuku Gyoen has about 1,000 cherry trees of some 65 varieties, flowering in turn from February to late April, and alcohol may not be brought in.

gives.name: The garden's weather
gives.text: The diary shows the next day hour by hour, and Kaede writes when rain is coming
gives.tip: Come to the shelter by the pond. It's the best seat in the garden when it rains.

options.text: The late double ones, when the crowds have gone
options.reply: A person after my own heart. The Ichiyo and the Kanzan open in mid April, when everyone has folded their blue sheets away.

options.text: The first week, with everyone else
options.reply: Then be at the gate at nine sharp. Or wait for the double ones in mid April: Ichiyo, Kanzan, and room to sit.

request.ask: Take more pictures in the good light, dear. Come back when you can tell me where the sun will be at four.

ranks.title: The pavilion from Taiwan
talk: The Kyu-Goryotei, across the water. Japanese residents of Taiwan gave it for a crown prince's wedding, and it was finished in 1927.
It's built in a southern Chinese style: look at the corners of the roof. That's why the maples here seem to belong to a painting from somewhere else.
ranks.fact: The Kyu-Goryotei, or Taiwan Pavilion, was given by Japanese residents of Taiwan to mark the wedding of the future Showa emperor and finished in 1927, in a southern Chinese style.

gives.name: Kaede's good word
gives.text: 10% more for every job in Shinjuku

ranks.title: Never the same twice
talk: I told you the pond is never the same twice. I should tell you why I started coming.
My husband and I meant to see it in every season. We managed spring. So I come for both of us, and on wet days I have it to myself.
Come when the maples turn, at the end of November. I'll keep you the dry end of the bench.
ranks.fact: The maples of Shinjuku Gyoen's Japanese garden turn red from late November into early December, among the last autumn colour in Tokyo.

gives.name: Kaede's way of looking
gives.text: Eye, from someone who looks slowly

bonds.title: The photographer on the footbridge
bonds.busy: Wrong light. I'm on the bridge at golden hour, when it's dry. A wet lens is no use to anyone.

ranks.title: The clock
ranks.invite: You looked up the street before you looked at me. Good sign. Have you some of the {slot}?
talk: That tower's a telephone exchange, really. Finished in 2000, 240 metres to the roof, and the upper floors are full of switching gear, not people.
The clock went on in 2002. Fifteen metres across. From here it's the size of the moon.
ranks.fact: The NTT Docomo Yoyogi Building, finished in 2000 and 240 m to its roof, gained its 15 m clock in 2002; most of its upper floors hold telecommunications equipment.

ask.q: When does the clock look its best?

options.text: Just after sunset, lit against a blue sky
options.reply: Yes. The face lights before the sky goes dark, and for ten minutes the two balance.
At midday it's a grey tower with a grey clock. Come just after sunset, when the lit face and the sky balance.

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Show me one frame taken in the good light: golden hour, or just after sunset.

ranks.title: Night film
talk: There. You waited, and it shows.
After dark I shoot the trains from here: the Chuo rapid and the Sobu local, four tracks in the cutting. I've set your camera the way I set mine for that. Cool, deep, the lamps kept white.
ranks.fact: Below the Shinanomachi footbridge the Chuo rapid and Chuo-Sobu local lines run on four tracks in a cutting along the edge of the Meiji Jingu Outer Garden.

gives.name: Night film
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Kenji's night stock

request.text: Photograph the three faces of the Outer Garden
request.ask: There's a small commission in your diary: three subjects round the Outer Garden. Do it properly.

ranks.title: The gallery
talk: The dome at the end of the avenue is the Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery. Finished in 1926: eighty big paintings of one emperor's reign, forty in the Japanese style and forty in the Western.
It's under scaffolding till 2027. Shoot it anyway. Buildings being mended are the honest ones.
ranks.fact: The Meiji Memorial Picture Gallery, completed in 1926, shows 80 large paintings of the Meiji emperor's reign, half in Japanese and half in Western style.

needs.text: Shoot more first. Come back when you can tell me which side of this bridge is in shadow at four.

request.text: Walk the ginkgo avenue at Jingu Gaien
request.ask: Have you walked the ginkgo avenue yet? Go to the Aoyama end and look back toward the dome.

ranks.title: A trick of the trees
talk: Did anything strike you about the ginkgos? They're planted by height: the tallest at the Aoyama end, the shortest by the gallery.
So the avenue looks longer than its three hundred metres, and the dome further off. Somebody composed my photograph a century before I took it.
ranks.fact: Jingu Gaien's 146 ginkgos are planted in order of height, tallest at the Aoyama-dori end, so the 300 m avenue looks longer toward the Picture Gallery.

ask.q: Where would you stand to shoot it?

options.text: At the Aoyama end, dead centre
options.reply: Dead centre, low, a long lens. Mind the taxis.
You'd get trees. Go to the Aoyama end, dead centre: that's where the trick is aimed.

gives.name: Kenji's eye
gives.text: Light, from someone who waits for it

ranks.title: One frame
talk: Same bridge every week, for six years. People ask what I'm waiting for.
A train on each of the four tracks, the clock on the hour, and the sky doing something. I've had three of the four, twice.
When I get it I'll stop coming, so I rather hope I don't. Find a bridge of your own somewhere.
ranks.fact: Shinanomachi Station opened in 1894 on the Kobu Railway, the private line that became the Chuo Line.

gives.name: A photographer's name
gives.text: 25% more for every job in Shinjuku

jobs.title: Which way from the east exit?
jobs.blurb: Visitors in the East Square ask the way. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.done: They bow, and set off the right way.

jobs.title: Kabukicho after dark
jobs.blurb: A travel magazine wants the red arch, the head over Central Road and the tower behind the plaza. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The picture editor writes back: 'The arch one. More like that.'

jobs.title: Three faces of the Outer Garden
jobs.blurb: For a calendar: the Docomo Tower's clock, the Picture Gallery's dome and the Shinanomachi footbridge. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: The calendar's printer wants the clock for November.

jobs.title: Skewers for Golden Gai
jobs.blurb: A box from Kenta's grill in Omoide Yokocho to Fumi's bar in Golden Gai, under the railway and up Yasukuni-dori, while they are hot.
jobs.text: Twenty skewers, half salt, half sauce. Keep the box level.
jobs.done: Fumi lifts the lid and nods.

jobs.title: A fare to Yotsuya
jobs.blurb: Drive your own car as a cab: pick up at the kerb by the east exit and take your passenger east along Shinjuku-dori to Yotsuya Station.
jobs.at_name: the kerb by the east exit
jobs.who: A lecturer with an armful of papers
jobs.text: "Yotsuya, the university side. My lecture starts on the hour."
jobs.done: "Keep the change. And slow down next time."

shops.name: A counter in Omoide Yokocho 思い出横丁
shops.where: Omoide Yokocho, by the west exit
shops.hello: Irasshai! Squeeze in. Salt or sauce?

menu.name: Motsu-yaki, two skewers
menu.text: Grilled pork offal, the lane's first dish: in 1946 offal was one of the few things a stall could sell off the ration. Salt first.

menu.name: Negima, two skewers
menu.text: Chicken thigh and leek, turn about, over charcoal. The leek is there to cut the fat, and you eat it straight off the stick.

menu.name: Motsu nikomi
menu.text: Offal stewed all day in miso with daikon and konnyaku, from a pot that is topped up and never emptied.

shops.name: Kissaten 喫茶店
shops.hello: Good morning. The set, or just coffee?

menu.name: Morning set
menu.text: Thick toast, a boiled egg and a cup of siphon coffee, served until eleven. The morning set is the old coffee shops' bargain: the food comes for the price of the coffee, or little more.

menu.name: Spaghetti Napolitan
menu.text: Soft spaghetti fried with ketchup, onion, green pepper and sausage. Nothing to do with Naples: it was made up in post-war Yokohama and never left the coffee shops.

menu.name: Mame daifuku
menu.text: Soft rice cake round sweet bean paste, with salted red peas in the skin. Made this morning; it will be hard by tomorrow, which is the point.

menu.name: Makunouchi bento
menu.text: Rice in neat barrels, grilled fish, a rolled omelette, simmered vegetables. The department store above opened in 1933; its basement food hall is where Tokyo buys its presents.

menu.name: Amazake
menu.text: A paper cup of sweet, thick rice drink, served hot. Shrines ladle it out at New Year and at winter festivals, and there is next to no alcohol in it.

menu.name: A small kumade
menu.text: A bamboo rake the size of your hand, hung with a gold coin and a rice bale, for raking in luck. At November's rooster fair people buy a bigger one each year.

events.title: Tori-no-ichi at Hanazono Shrine
events.text: The rooster fair: on the days of the rooster in November, and the eve of each, the shrine sells bamboo rakes for luck until midnight. The dates move every year; these are 2026's.
lines: A wall of paper lanterns at the gate, each with a sponsor's name, and behind it stalls stacked to the roof with bamboo rakes: gold coins, rice bales, sea bream, masks.
Somebody has bought a big one. The whole stall claps it out for them, three-three-three-one, and the buyer carries it off held high, so the luck doesn't spill.
The fair falls on the days of the rooster in November: two in most years, three in some. In 2026 they are the 7th and the 19th, with an eve before each.

events.title: Cherries in Shinjuku Gyoen
events.text: About a thousand cherry trees of some sixty-five kinds. The Somei-Yoshino are at their best around the turn of April in most years; no alcohol is allowed in.
lines: Picnic sheets on the lawns, and not a can of beer among them: bags are checked at the gates. You can hear the petals land.
About a thousand trees of some sixty-five kinds. The pale Somei-Yoshino go first, around the turn of April in most years; the double Ichiyo and Kanzan carry on to the end of the month.

events.title: Shinjuku Eisa Festival
events.where: The east exit and the streets round the station
events.text: Okinawa's Bon dance, drummed through the streets on both sides of the station on the last Saturday of July: the 25th in 2026.
lines: You hear it from inside the station: barrel drums and hand drums, a sanshin over a loudspeaker, and a shout on every fourth beat.
Some twenty troupes, more than a thousand dancers, drumming as they march. Eisa is how Okinawa sees its ancestors off at Bon; Shinjuku has borrowed it on the last Saturday of July since 2002.

events.title: Jingu Gaien fireworks
events.where: Jingu Gaien, by the ginkgo avenue
events.text: About ten thousand shells over the stadiums of the Outer Garden, from 19:30 for an hour, on a Saturday in August in most years: the 8th in 2026.
lines: Yukata on the avenue, fans in every belt, and nobody looking where they walk. The first shell goes up at half past seven.
About ten thousand shells in an hour, fired from among the stadiums. These are the only big fireworks you can watch from the middle of the city, and half of Aoyama watches from its roofs.

events.title: Ginkgo festival at Jingu Gaien
events.text: The avenue's 146 ginkgos turn from mid November and are at their yellowest at the end of the month in most years; for about a week they are lit from 16:30.
lines: Four rows of ginkgos clipped to points, and the pavement the same yellow as the trees. People walk down the middle of the road with their phones held up.
146 trees, tallest at this end and shortest by the gallery, so the avenue looks longer than it is. At the end of November they are lit for about a week, from half past four.
